message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, etc.).
• Texas Property Code §92.001–92.006 covers “unlawful detainer” and habitability. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to fix major issues, you may withhold rent or repair‑and‑deduct (but only for certain repairs). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice of entry. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, you must follow the lease terms or the landlord must provide a valid reason for early termination. | • Provide written notice and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a **notice** (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease violation).
• If you don’t comply, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, you have the right to contest it in court. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • Texas law allows tenants to repair a problem and deduct the cost from rent **only** if the landlord fails to fix a major issue within a reasonable time. | • Document the issue, send a written notice, and keep receipts. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities (water, heat, electricity). | • Verify which utilities you’re responsible for in the lease. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Lease may restrict subletting; if allowed, you must follow the lease terms. | • Get landlord’s written consent before subletting. | | **Insurance** | • Landlord is not required to provide renter’s insurance, but you may want it for personal belongings. | • Consider a renter’s insurance policy. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If your rights are violated, you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, the Texas Commission on Human Rights, or the local housing agency. | • Keep all documentation (emails, texts, photos). | ### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Read the lease carefully** – note rent amount, due date, security deposit, pet policy, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Document the unit’s condition** – take dated photos or videos. 3. **Ask for a written receipt** of the security deposit. 4. **Know your local ordinances** – some cities have additional tenant protections (e.g., rent control, eviction moratoria). ### When Problems Arise - **Write a formal complaint** to the landlord. - **Keep copies** of all correspondence. - **Contact a local tenant‑rights group** (e.g., Texas Tenants Union, local legal aid). - **Consider mediation** before going to court. --- #### Resources - **Texas Property Code** – the statutory basis for most tenant rights. - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – for discrimination complaints. - **Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division** – for landlord‑tenant disputes. - **Local legal aid organizations** – free or low‑cost legal help. If you have a specific issue (e.g., a dispute over a security deposit, a repair that hasn’t been made, or an eviction notice), let me know and I can give more targeted guidance.
